title: Accusative Case
summary: The accusative case is used for the direct object in a sentence. It answers the question 'Wen?' or 'Was?'. In beginner German, it is usually the first case learners notice because some articles and pronouns change when the noun becomes the object.
whyItMatters: You need the accusative to say what someone sees, buys, has, likes, or does to something. Without it, many everyday German sentences feel incomplete or incorrect.

ruleBlocks.title: Main use
ruleBlocks.content: Use the accusative for the direct object — the person or thing directly affected by the action.

ruleBlocks.title: Question clue
ruleBlocks.content: The accusative often answers the question 'Wen?' (whom?) or 'Was?' (what?).

ruleBlocks.title: Important article change
ruleBlocks.content: In the accusative, the masculine article usually changes. 'der' becomes 'den' and 'ein' becomes 'einen'. Feminine, neuter, and plural often stay the same in the article form at this level.

examples.note: The verb 'sehen' takes a direct object. 'der Mann' becomes 'den Mann'.

patterns: Subject + modal verb + accusative object + infinitive
tips: At A1 level, the fastest clue is this: if the noun is masculine, check whether the article changes to 'den' or 'einen'.
If the action is done directly to a person or thing, accusative is very common.
Learn accusative together with verbs you use daily: sehen, haben, kaufen, brauchen, lieben.

memoryHooks.title: Think 'target of the action'
memoryHooks.content: The accusative is often the target that receives the action directly.

memoryHooks.title: Masculine is the warning sign
memoryHooks.content: When you see a masculine noun, slow down and check whether the article must change.

commonMistakes.reason: Masculine definite article changes in the accusative.
Personal pronouns also change in the accusative.
Masculine indefinite article changes from 'ein' to 'einen'.

sourceStyle.notes: This is a learner-friendly synthesized explanation aligned to beginner German teaching patterns, not a verbatim copy from one school.
